U.S. Patent Application 20230277119 (Lewinson et al.) discloses a system that detects skin contact reactions to a set of allergens. During operation, the system enables a user to acquire an image of a patch area through a camera in a portable device, wherein the patch area is located on the skin of a patient, and wherein a patch containing the set of allergens is applied to the patch area for a period of time and removed before the image is acquired. Next, the system preprocesses the image so that a resulting preprocessed image of the patch area has a prespecified size and orientation. The system then performs image-processing operations on the preprocessed image to identify regions of the patch area corresponding to positive skin contact reactions. The system labels each identified region with a specific allergen that is applied to the region to produce test results, which identify specific allergens that produced positive skin contact reactions.

Allergic contact dermatitis (ACD) is a chronic condition that produces erythematous (red), pruritic (itchy), painful, eczematous rashes, sometimes also associated with skin blisters or fissures (cracks). ACD is the result of a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to an allergen, which typically occurs 48 to 72 hours after exposure. Patch testing entails having a series of

patches which contain an individual allergen suspended in petrolatum gel (or another medium) applied to the skin, typically on the upper back, for approximately 48 hours. The results of this exposure (delayed hypersensitivity reaction) are assessed after an additional 48 to 72 hours.

U.S. Patent No. 5551441 (Pitesky) discloses an injection pick holder for testing a plurality of different allergens on a patient. The injection pick holder includes a vial holder that is cooperatively engageable with a vial tray. The vial holder includes a plurality of vertical stems that cooperatively engage with a plurality of upwardly opening vial receptacle tubes each filled with an allergen. The vial holder includes a pair of upwardly and outwardly angling grasping ears for use in opening longitudinal slits in the vial tray which open jaw sockets in the vial tray during allergen loading. The mechanism for penetrating the skin of the patient is a plurality of sharp points, circularly arranged about a center and generally evenly spaced for each allergen. The allergen is applied to the patient through a plurality of picks disposed in a common plane which simultaneously press against and prick the skin of a patient. The vial holder applies a downward force on the skin of the patient to enable downward projecting applicator picks to puncture the skin and place the allergens under the skin of the patient. The puncture method is accomplished by piercing the patient's skin with sharply pointed prongs while applying a drop of allergen. Several devices have been developed which apply a plurality of allergens simultaneously at predetermined spaced apart locations on the patient's skin. By applying all of the allergens simultaneously, these device are effective in reducing the duration of discomfort of the patient and have been successfully used in situations using the puncture technique has been the desired method of application. It is noted that the Pitesky reference makes no reference to image capture and analysis. Accordingly, if Applicants can distinguish from the Lewinson reference in this regard, the individual references and their combination will be overcome.

The invention, as now claimed, is an augmented reality automated allergy system that selects a test site upon the skin of the patient that is relatively clear of discoloration to configure treatment for addressing allergy issues of a patient. The system comprises a multiple test applicator, a smart phone or a tablet computer,
and a computer-generated treatment plan.

The multiple test applicator is cooperatively engageable with a fluid tray during allergen loading, and cooperatively engageable with skin of the patient during allergen deposition. The multiple test applicator delivers a trace amount of a first allergen to a first test site and a trace amount of a second allergen to a second test site during the allergen deposition.

A first smart phone or a first tablet computer captures a first image of the first and the second test sites. Either the first smart phone or the first tablet computer or a second smart phone or a tablet computer captures a second image of the first and second tests site 15 to 20 minutes after the allergen deposition. The second image is captured after the first image is captured. the first allergy condition being detectable as a first wheal forms at the first test site. An allergy determination is based on a comparison of the second image of the first and the second test sites with the first image of the first and the second test sites.

Preferably, the first image is captured immediately after the allergen deposition. And preferably, the analysis at the first and second test sites are completed within 30 minutes of the allergen deposition.

The computer-generated treatment plan is generated using machine learning, the computer-generated treatment plan is a step-by-step procedure for a medical professional. The computer-generated treatment plan is stored in a medical database for treating patients with the first allergy condition.

Claims 1-24 are rejected under 35 USC §112(b) or 35 USC §112 (pre-AIA), second paragraph, as being indefinite for failing to particularly point out and distinctly claim the subject matter which the joint inventors regards as the invention. In the subject Office Action Claims 1-24 are rejected under 35 USC §112(a) or 35 USC §112 (pre-AIA), first paragraph, as failing to comply with the written description requirement. The claims contains subject matter which was not described in the specification in such a way as to reasonably convey to one skilled in the relevant art that the inventor or a joint inventor, or for applications subject to pre-AIA 35 USC §112, the inventor(s), at the time the application was filed, had possession of the claimed invention.

In the subject Office Action Claim 1 recites "develop[ing] a computer-generated treatment plan using machine learning for said patient having said first allergy condition, said computer-generated treatment plan being a step-by-step procedure for a medical professional, said patient having an electronic medical record, said computer-generated treatment plan being stored in a medical database for treating patients with said first allergy condition".

Similarly, in the subject Office Action Claim 9 recites "a computer-generated treatment plan for treating said patient having said first allergy condition, said computer-generated treatment plan being generated using machine learning, said computer-generated treatment plan being a step-by-step procedure for a medical professional, said patient having an electronic medical record, said computer- generated treatment plan being stored in a medical database for treating patients with said first allergy condition".
Also, in the subject Office Action Claim 17 recites "a computer-generated treatment plan for said patient having said first allergy condition, said computer-generated treatment

plan being generated using machine learning, said patient having an electronic medical record, said computer-generated treatment plan being a step-by-step procedure for a medical professional, said computer-generated treatment plan being stored in a medical database for treating patients with said first allergy condition". The subject Office Action states that Claims 1-24 fail to satisfy the written description requirement because "the invention is claimed and described in functional language, but the specification does not sufficiently identify how the invention achieves the claimed function. Ariad, 598 F.3d at 1349, 94 USPQ2d at 1171 ("An adequate written description of a claimed genus requires more than a generic statement of an invention's boundaries.") (citing Eli Lilly, 119 F.3d at 1568, 43 USPQ2d at 1405-06)." MPEP §2161.01.

"When examining computer-implemented functional claims, examiners should determine whether the specification discloses the computer and the algorithm (e.g., the necessary steps and/or flowcharts) that perform the claimed function in sufficient detail such that one of ordinary skill in the art can reasonably conclude that the
inventor invented the claimed subject matter." Id.

"[F]or computer-implemented inventions, the determination of the sufficiency of disclosure will require an inquiry into both the sufficiency of the disclosed hardware as well as the disclosed software due to the interrelationship and
interdependence of computer hardware and software." Id.

"If the specification does not provide a disclosure of the computer and algorithm in sufficient detail to demonstrate to one of ordinary skill in the art that the inventor possessed theinvention including how to program the disclosed compute, to perform the claimed function, a rejection under 35 USC §112{a) or pre-AIA 35 USC §112, first
paragraph, for lack of written description must be made." Id.

The subject Office Action further states that although examples are cited in Pages 16-22 and 36-38 of the Applicant's Specification, this does not provide sufficient detail for the steps of "developing a computer-generated treatment plan using machine learning for said patient having said first allergy condition, said computer-generated treatment plan being a step-by-step procedure for a medical professional, said patient having an electronic medical record, said computer-generated treatment plan being stored in a medical database for treating patients with said first allergy condition". Specifically, the specification does not explain the programming or describe the exact hardware needed for developing a computer-generated treatment plan using machine learning for said patient having said first allergy condition.

On Page 21 of the Applicant's Specification, Applicant cites Devarakonda et al (U.S. Patent Serial No. 16/018301), which discloses a mechanism provided in a data processing system comprising a processor and a memory, wherein the memory comprises instructions that are executed by the processor to specifically configure the processor to implement a cognitive analysis engine for analysis and disambiguation of electronic medical records for presentation of pertinent information for a medical treatment plan. Although Devarakonda discloses an invention that utilizes some type of machine learning, the field of machine learning is very broad, and there are no specific teachings regarding how this technology can be used in this specific application-used with viewing devices, multiple test applicator, computer-generated treatment plan, or allergy systems.

The specification does not sufficiently identify how the invention achieves the claimed function and therefore fails to satisfy the written description requirement.

VII - THE 103 REJECTION
Claims 1-2, 6-7, 9, 13-15, 17, and 21-23 are rejected under 35 USC §103 as being unpatentable over Lewinson et al (U.S. Publication No. 2023/0277119) in view of Pitesky (U.S. Patent No. 5,551,441).

Independent Claims 1, 9, and 17 have been substantially redrafted in lieu of the Lewinson reference. Applicants had not seen it before. The publication date of the Lewinson reference is September 7, 2023. Lewinson was not published until after the parent application of the present Patent Application (now U.S. Patent No. 11,911,172) was filed. There are substantial differences between Applicants' invention and Lewinson. The Claims have now been amended to distinguish from this reference. Applicants' system deploys a multiple test applicator. The multiple test applicator is loaded with multiple allergens during an allergen loading process where the multiple test applicator is cooperatively engaged with a loading tray. The multiple test applicator then becomes cooperatively engaged with the skin of the patient during an allergen deposition process.

By contrast, Lewinson deploys a new technique for diagnosing ACD and identifying associated allergens using patch testing techniques. ACD is the result of a delayed hypersensitivity reaction to an allergen, which typically occurs 48 to 72 hours after exposure. Patch testing entails having a series of patches which contain an individual allergen suspended in petrolatum gel or other medium applied to the skin, typically on the upper back, for approximately 48 hours. The results of this exposure are assessed after an additional 48 to 72 hours.
Applicants' independent Claims 1 and 9 now include the following limitation:
"capturing a second image of said first test site and said second test site within 15 to 20 minutes after said allergen deposition . . . . , said second image being captured after
said first image is captured"
Applicants' independent Claim 17 now includes the following limitation:

"means for capturing a second image of said first test site and said second test site 15 to 20 minutes after said allergen deposition, ...., said second image being captured after said first image has been captured, said first allergy condition being detectable as a first wheal forms at said first test site, an analysis being based upon a comparison of said second image of said first test site and said second test site with said first image of said
first test site and said second test site"

An analysis is performed in Applicants' system. The analysis is based upon a comparison of the second image of the first and second test sites with the first image of the first and second test sites. We have not seen this before and we believe that this is novel. Test results are available in a matter of minutes, rather 2 or 3 days. In contrast to the teaching of Lewinson, patch testing entails having a series of patches which contain an individual allergen suspended in petrolatum gel (or another medium) applied to the skin, typically on the upper back, for approximately 48 hours. The results of this exposure (delayed hypersensitivity reaction) are assessed after an additional 48 to 72 hours.

An invention that would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill at the time of the invention is not patentable. As reiterated by the Supreme Court in KSR, the framework for the objective analysis for determining obviousness under 35 USC §103 is stated in Graham v. John Deere Co., 383 U.S. 1. Obviousness is a question of law based on underlying factual inquiries. The basic factual inquiries of Graham v. John Deere Co. (see MPEP §2141),
(A) Determining the scope and content of the prior art;
(B) Ascertaining the differences between the claimed invention and the prior art; and
(C) Resolving the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art.

In rejecting claims under 35 USC §103, the examiner bears the initial burden of presenting a prima facie case of obviousness. In re Oetiker, 977 F.2d 1443, 1445, (Fed.Cir.1992). Only if that burden is met, does the burden of coming forward with evidence or argument shift to the applicant. Id. "A prima facie case of obviousness is established when the teachings from the prior art itself would appear to have suggested the claimed subject matter to a person of ordinary skill in the art." In re Bell, 991 F.2d 781, 782, (Fed.Cir.1993) (quoting In re Rinehart, 531 F.2d 1048, 1051, (CCPA 1976)). If the examiner fails to establish a prima facie case, the rejection is improper and will be overturned. In re Fine, 837 F.2d 1071, 1074, (Fed.Cir.1988).
